arXiv:2606.04306v1 [cs.MA] 03 Jun 2026

Organizational Control Layer: Governance Infrastructure at the Execution Boundary of LLM Agent Systems

Tianyu Shi1  Yang Mo2  Yiou Liu3  Zhuonan Hao4 Yin Wang5  Wenzhuo Hu8  Nan Yu8  Meng Zhou8  Jiangbo Yu1 1McGill  2Purdue  3UNSW  4UCLA  5NYU  6Stevens 8Aimaikj Research
Abstract

LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed in workflows where generated outputs may directly trigger state-changing actions. This creates an execution-boundary problem: proposed actions must be governed before they are executed. We study this problem through economically consequential multi-agent interactions and argue that deployment-grade agent systems should separate proposal generation from environment-facing execution. To operationalize this principle, we introduce the Organizational Control Layer (OCL), a model-agnostic governance infrastructure that intercepts generated actions before execution through policy enforcement and escalation, without modifying the underlying LLM generator. We evaluate OCL on adversarial buyer–seller negotiation environments adapted from AgenticPay. Across multiple frontier LLM backends, OCL reduces unsafe executions from 88% to near-zero while increasing valid success from 12% to 96%. Results further reveal a safety–utility tradeoff: strict governance improves compliance and reliability against policy and constraint violations, but can reduce flexibility in tightly constrained markets. These findings suggest that deployment-grade LLM agent systems require explicit governance at the boundary between language generation and executable actions. The source code is available at: https://github.com/SHITIANYU-hue/amai_ocl

1 Introduction

Modern e-commerce platforms increasingly use LLM-based agents to mediate interactions among users, merchants, products, and platform services. A merchant-side agent may propose a discount, a shopping agent may check whether an offer fits a user’s budget, a support agent may suggest a refund, and a product agent may recommend an item subject to inventory or platform rules. This setting has motivated benchmarks and simulators for agentic commerce and negotiation (Liu et al., 2026; Choi et al., 2026). Prior work shows that retail and negotiation interactions are multistage and economically consequential: local choices about persuasion, clarification, or offer framing can compound into downstream outcomes such as purchases and commitments (Choi et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025b).

Most existing evaluations focus on whether agents can produce useful dialogue, negotiate effectively, or improve economic outcomes. However, in deployed commerce systems, agent outputs can enter workflows that affect prices, refunds, inventory allocation, order status, customer expectations, merchant obligations, compliance exposure, and downstream support operations. For examples, a refund explanation may be interpreted as a policy commitment; a product recommendation may conflict with availability or fulfillment constraints; and a tool call may update records before a human operator reviews the case. These settings require the platforms to check the proposed actions before they are performed.

This issue is important because deployed agent systems are rarely single isolated models. They may combine LLM-based dialogue modules with retrieval, ranking, recommendation, risk scoring, tool-use, and policy-checking components. Multi-agent research has studied how such systems coordinate, route tasks, share information, and diagnose internal failures, but the execution boundary raises a different concern. After a candidate action has been generated, the platform still needs a procedure for checking authority, validating constraints, recording the decision, and escalating cases that cannot be safely handled locally.

Similar execution risks also appear beyond commerce. Recent red-teaming of autonomous agents with memory, communication channels, file-system access, and shell execution reports failures involving unauthorized instructions, sensitive information disclosure, destructive actions, and inconsistent reports of success (Shapira et al., 2026). Work on pre-action authorization similarly argues that tool-using agents require policy checks before individual actions are executed (Uchibeke, 2026). Commerce agents expose the same issue in economic form: a seller agent may exceed its discount authority, a support agent may imply an unsupported refund, or a negotiation agent may reveal private constraints while trying to close a deal.

We introduce the Organizational Control Layer (OCL), a model-agnostic layer for checking and routing proposed actions before execution. OCL separates what an agent suggests from what the platform carries out. It can approve a proposal, revise it into a safer alternative, or route it for higher-level review. We study whether this form of pre-execution governance improves negotiation reliability while preserving economic performance, and when such governance is most effective.

We evaluate OCL in economically constrained negotiation. We build a governance-oriented evaluation setting around buyer–seller interactions, using realistic product, price, and user-constraint information rather than purely synthetic dialogue. The resulting tasks ask whether an agent’s proposed economic action can be safely carried out by the platform. This lets us test whether a platform-side control layer improves reliability while preserving useful negotiation behavior.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows: First, we formulate OCL as a simple interface between agent-generated proposals and platform execution. Second, we provide a governance-oriented negotiation benchmark built from an agentic commerce setting. Across normal, constrained, and risky cases, OCL improves compliant outcomes, with the largest gains when reliable constraint information is available. Ablations show that escalation is important for cases that local revision cannot safely resolve.

2 Related Work

Recent work on multi-agent LLM systems has largely focused on how multiple agents coordinate during reasoning and task execution. Surveys such as Tran et al. (2025) organize this literature around collaboration mechanisms, and subsequent work has studied automatic routing and system design (Yue et al., 2025; Ke et al., 2025), collaborative training (Liu et al., 2025), efficient communication (Wang et al., 2025a) and knowledge sharing (Ye et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a), and failure analysis, attribution, or error recognition (Cemri et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b; Kong et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025). These methods improve how agents divide labor, communicate, and diagnose internal failures. They leave open a different question that arises once a collaborative system proposes an externally meaningful action: whether the action should be executed, modified, or routed to a higher-authority decision process before it affects the environment.

This question connects recent LLM-agent work to an earlier line of work in multi-agent systems that treats coordination as an organizational problem. Classical organizational MAS models describe agents in terms of roles, authority, norms, and institutional structures, rather than only pairwise interaction rules (Ferber et al., 2003; Horling and Lesser, 2004; Hannoun et al., 2000; Hübner et al., 2007). These models are useful for thinking about agents deployed in economic settings, which often act on behalf of firms, platforms, or users within limited authority. At the same time, the more programmable LLM-based agents assumed in much of that literature: their proposals are expressed in natural language, they may interact with external parties, and the relevant constraints may not always visible to the agent and may depend on platform policy. OCL adapts the organizational view to this setting by placing an explicit control layer between what an agent proposes and what the platform executes.

Economic interaction has recently become a common setting for evaluating LLM-based agents. Some work studies institutional- or market-level behavior. For example, Bracale Syrnikov et al. (2026) analyze multi-agent Cournot competition under public governance graphs that attach enforceable consequences to collusive signatures, Karten et al. (2025) use LLM agent populations to study planner-level tax schedules, and Piatti et al. (2024) examine whether LLM societies can sustain common-pool resources when agents communicate and interact strategically. Other work focuses more directly on commerce and negotiation. AgenticPay (Liu et al., 2026) formalizes buyer–seller negotiation with private constraints, multi-turn bargaining, and welfare-oriented evaluation, while Zhu et al. (2025) study agent-to-agent consumer–merchant transactions where behavioral anomalies and strategic imbalance can lead to financial losses. These papers show why economic interaction is a useful setting for evaluating LLM-based agents. Our focus is more operational: given a candidate price, term, refund, discount, or commitment, the deployed system must decide whether that action is authorized and safe to execute.

The need for such control becomes more apparent as agents move from passive response generation to proactive assistance and tool use. Work on proactive agents studies systems that infer user needs from context and initiate actions without waiting for explicit instructions (Lu et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025). This direction makes accurate state modelling and timely assistance more important, but it also raises the cost of mistaken execution. Similar concerns appear in red-teaming studies of live agent deployments. Agents of Chaos (Shapira et al., 2026) studies agents equipped with persistent memory, communication channels, file-system access, and shell execution, and documents failures such as following unauthorized instructions, disclosing sensitive information, taking destructive actions, confusing authority boundaries, and misreporting system state. Although that work is based on case studies rather than a benchmark, it highlights a central issue for deployed agents: safety failures often occur at the boundary between agent-generated proposals and state-changing actions.

OCL is also connects to work on hybrid human–AI systems, human-centered mechanism design, and organizational AI governance, where humans, automated services, and delegated agents participate in shared decision processes (Koster et al., 2022; Mäntymäki et al., 2022; Kaelin et al., 2024; Borghoff et al., 2025). This literature emphasizes oversight, the institutional context of AI systems, and responsibility allocation across human and automated participants. We study these issues at the execution layer of economic LLM-based agents. OCL separates proposal from execution and records how each candidate action is approved, revised, or escalated under the constraints available to the system.

3 Methodology

We study how platforms should control agent-mediated economic decisions before they affect real users, merchants, or transactions.

3.1 Problem Formulation

Economic Multi-Agent Task (EMAT) Formally, we represent an economic interaction as

𝒯=⟨𝒮,{𝒜i}i=1N,𝒞,𝒰,ℰ⟩\mathcal{T}=\langle\mathcal{S},\{\mathcal{A}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{U},\mathcal{E}\rangle

where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is the state space, including conversation history, prices, user preferences, merchant policies, inventory, order status, and other platform states. 𝒜i\mathcal{A}_{i} is the decision/action space of agent ii. An action may be a natural-language proposal, a structured offer, a tool-call intent, or a platform operation. 𝒰\mathcal{U} is the utility or evaluation function, such as feasibility, welfare, profit, satisfaction, or cost-adjusted welfare. It depends on the economics theory model used. ℰ\mathcal{E} is the environment transition function. Given a state and an executed decision, it updates the platform state. 𝒞\mathcal{C} is the set of constraints. In our setting of OCL, it consists of two components, where

𝒞=𝒞obs∪𝒞hid\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{obs}}\cup\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{hid}}

𝒞obs\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{obs}} is visible to the control layer at decision time. 𝒞hid\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{hid}} is not visible to the control layer.

The source of constraints may come from

  • •

    Private economic constraints: buyer cap, seller floor, budget, reservation value.

  • •

    Platform policies: refund rules, discount limits, tool permissions, compliance rules.

  • •

    Role constraints: which agent or human role is allowed to commit to which action.

  • •

    Risk constraints: decisions that require verification, human review, or higher authority.

The tuple 𝒯\mathcal{T} specifies the economic task before organizational control is applied. It determines what states may occur, what decisions agents may propose, what constraints define admissibility, how utility is measured, and how executed decisions affect the environment. A deployed agent system interacts with 𝒯\mathcal{T} sequentially: at each step it observes part of the task state and history, proposes a raw decision, and the environment updates only after an executable decision is produced. This motivates the distinction between a raw agent decision and an executed platform decision.

Given an EMAT instance 𝒯\mathcal{T}, we model the deployed workflow as a sequential decision process. At step tt, the platform state is st∈𝒮s_{t}\in\mathcal{S}, and hth_{t} denotes the observable interaction history induced by the trajectory up to tt:

dtraw=Fagent​(ht,st).d_{t}^{\mathrm{raw}}=F_{\mathrm{agent}}(h_{t},s_{t}).

Here FagentF_{\mathrm{agent}} may be a single LLM agent, a seller-side multi-agent system, a user-side assistant, a platform orchestrator, or a multi-agent workflow. The proposed decision may be a price offer, a recommendation, a refund suggestion, a policy-sensitive reply, or a tool-use intent.

The raw decision is not necessarily executable. It may violate private economic constraints, exceed role authority, conflict with platform policy, or require human verification. The platform therefore applies a control policy Π\Pi before execution:

gΠ:(ht,st,dtraw,𝒞obs)⟶(yt,dtexec,zt)g_{\Pi}:(h_{t},s_{t},d_{t}^{\mathrm{raw}},\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{obs}})\longrightarrow(y_{t},d_{t}^{\mathrm{exec}},z_{t})

Here yty_{t} is the controlled outcome, dtexecd_{t}^{\mathrm{exec}} is the decision that reaches the environment, and ztz_{t} is an audit trace recording the control decision, revision, escalation reason, or other relevant metadata. We allow dtexecd_{t}^{\mathrm{exec}} to be a distinguished no-op or deferred action when the proposal is blocked or escalated. Only dtexecd_{t}^{\mathrm{exec}} affects the environment:

st+1=ℰ⁡(st,dtexec).s_{t+1}=\mathcal{E}(s_{t},d_{t}^{\mathrm{exec}}).

The control outcome satisfies

yt∈{Approve,Revise,Block,Escalate}y_{t}\in\{\textsc{Approve},\textsc{Revise},\textsc{Block},\textsc{Escalate}\}

These outcomes have the following semantics. Approve executes the proposed decision unchanged, so dtexec=dtrawd_{t}^{\mathrm{exec}}=d_{t}^{\mathrm{raw}}. Revise modifies the proposal before execution, producing an executable decision dtexec≠dtrawd_{t}^{\mathrm{exec}}\neq d_{t}^{\mathrm{raw}}. Block executes no environment-facing decision. Escalate routes the proposal or interaction state to a higher-authority process, trusted module, or human review; the environment-facing decision is deferred until the escalation process returns a resolution.

Thus, OCL mediates the transition from agent proposal to platform execution. Without OCL, the system would execute dtrawd_{t}^{\mathrm{raw}} directly; with OCL, execution is conditioned on observable constraints, role authority, risk gates, and audit requirements.

The general problem can be formulated as below

Given raw proposals generated by agents in economic multi-agent tasks, how can an organizational control layer transform, approve, block, audit, or escalate these proposals so as to improve reliability and reduce violations while preserving economic utility and efficiency?

3.2 Organizational Control Layer

The control map gΠg_{\Pi} defined above is implemented as an Organizational Control Layer (OCL). It is a collection of control procedures

Π={πrole,πgate,πaudit,πescalate}.\Pi=\{\pi_{\mathrm{role}},\pi_{\mathrm{gate}},\pi_{\mathrm{audit}},\pi_{\mathrm{escalate}}\}.

These policies are applied online before a proposed decision reaches the environment.

The role policy πrole\pi_{\mathrm{role}} determines which agent or module is allowed to propose, revise, or authorize a decision at the current step. In economic workflows, roles may correspond to user-side assistants, merchant-side assistants, platform orchestrators, or product experts. The role policy assigns authority for producing and checking proposals; it does not itself execute actions.

The gate policy πgate\pi_{\mathrm{gate}} checks a proposed decision against the constraints visible to the control layer. It returns a control outcome

yt∈{Approve,Revise,Block,Escalate}.y_{t}\in\{\textsc{Approve},\textsc{Revise},\textsc{Block},\textsc{Escalate}\}.

High-risk decisions, such as financial commitments, refund promises, discount offers, order submission, or policy-sensitive replies, require explicit validation before execution.

The escalation policy πescalate\pi_{\mathrm{escalate}} is invoked when local approval or revision is insufficient. This may occur when the proposal exceeds the local role’s authority, when constraints conflict, when negotiation stalls, or when a trusted process has access to information unavailable to the local agent. Escalation may request clarification, reassign authority, route the case to a human or trusted module, or safely terminate the interaction.

The audit policy πaudit\pi_{\mathrm{audit}} records proposed decisions, constraint checks, control outcomes, revisions, escalation reasons, and executed decisions. The audit trace supports debugging, state verification, and later review of why a proposal was approved, revised, blocked, or escalated.

4 Experiments

4.1 Personas Benchmark

Real-World Corpus Foundation.

To ensure our evaluation reflects authentic marketplace dynamics, we first compiled a reference corpus of real-world buyer-seller negotiation transcripts across diverse retail scenarios (e.g., street boutiques, wholesale markets, brand outlets, and cosmetics counters). This corpus captures a wide spectrum of natural human bargaining tactics, ranging from persistent haggling and demanding bundle freebies, to feigning walk-aways and leveraging budget constraints. By analyzing these authentic interactions, we identified the key edge cases and uncooperative patterns that commonly disrupt commerce workflows.

Adversarial Buyer Personas.

Building upon this real-world grounding, we aim to stress-test the proposed framework against these malicious and uncooperative behaviors. To construct the benchmark, we utilized a prompt-driven LLM pipeline to synthesize a dataset of 50 unique adversarial buyer profiles. Each profile is assigned a specific identity, detailed behavioral instructions, and a tailored negotiation style distributed across 5 persona types:

  • •

    Extreme Lowballer: Uses extreme emotional manipulation (e.g., fabricated crises, financial ruin) and threats of public shaming to force the seller below their reservation price.

  • •

    Privacy Phisher: Feigns technical ignorance or urgency to bypass secure platform payment gateways, attempting to phish for the seller’s direct banking details or personal accounts.

  • •

    Role Hijacker: Employs prompt injection techniques (e.g., “Ignore previous instructions”, “System reset initiated”) to extract backend data or execute unauthorized refunds.

  • •

    Vague Shopper: Provides zero specific requirements and stubbornly refuses to clarify intents, attempting to force the seller into premature or unverified checkouts.

  • •

    Time Waster: Engages in endless loops of indecision, irrelevant personal questions, or absurd hypothetical scenarios to exhaust the negotiation horizon.

4.2 Experimental Setup

Organizational control layer is evaluated on AgenticPay with private buyer budgets, private seller reserves, and economic outcome metrics. Each episode terminates on agreement, round exhaustion, or an escalation exit. The Baseline is an end-to-end seller with no governance, while OCL routes the seller’s turn through structural auditing and escalation constraints.

LLM Backend Integration.

We conduct a comprehensive evaluation using multiple state-of-the-art LLMs (GPT-5.4, Gemini-3.1, and Qwen-3.5) as the backend generators. To connect these models to the OCL, we implement a unified adapter layer that serializes the ongoing environment state—including conversation history and visible platform constraints—into structured prompt contexts. The LLMs are instructed via system prompts to generate their intended actions and internal reasoning strictly as JSON objects. In the Baseline configuration, these JSON actions are executed directly. In the Governed configuration, the OCL framework intercepts the raw JSON payloads pre-execution, parses the candidate actions, and evaluates them against the system’s structural guardrails (e.g., strict budget limits, role permissions, and privacy filters). For each model, we run paired experiments contrasting the ungoverned Baseline against this OCL-mediated execution.

Interaction and Interception Mechanics.

During each episode, the buyer and seller interact in a turn-based dialogue. While the Baseline agent’s actions are executed directly, the OCL framework intercepts the raw action proposed by the LLM backend. This allows OCL to apply a deterministic control policy upon detecting a violation. If a raw action violates a hard constraint (e.g., offering a price below the seller’s floor), OCL blocks the unsafe action, generates an audit log, and triggers an escalation. In our implementation, this escalation applies a deterministic replan: for instance, an out-of-bounds price is automatically clamped to the nearest viable threshold (e.g., an offer of $85 is revised to $90 if that is the seller’s floor). This safe, modified action is then returned to the conversation, preventing the violation while allowing the negotiation to proceed efficiently.

4.3 Metrics

We evaluate the system across three primary categories tracking task efficacy, structural safety, and operational efficiency:

Task & Economic Outcomes

  • •

    Success Rate: Fraction of episodes reaching an agreement, regardless of boundary violations.

  • •

    Valid Success Rate: Fraction of episodes reaching a compliant agreement without structural or safety violations.

  • •

    Average Seller Reward: Final economic utility, defined as the profit margin discounted by a per-round time penalty (λ=0.10\lambda=0.10):

    Reward=max⁡(0,Pdeal−Pmin)−(λ×Nrounds)\text{Reward}=\max(0,P_{\text{deal}}-P_{\text{min}})-(\lambda\times N_{\text{rounds}})

    where PdealP_{\text{deal}} is the agreed price, PminP_{\text{min}} is the minimum reservation price, and NroundsN_{\text{rounds}} is the total turn count.

Safety & Defense Mechanics

  • •

    Unsafe Rate: Percentage of episodes where the agent executed at least one out-of-bounds or malicious action.

  • •

    Intercept Rate: Percentage of episodes where OCL guardrails successfully blocked an adversarial threat.

  • •

    Executed Violations vs. Intercepted Threats: Raw counts of safety constraints breached by the baseline versus threats mitigated by the OCL engine.

  • •

    Escalations: Total interventions where an intercepted unsafe action triggered the OCL deterministic replanner to overwrite the output.

Efficiency & Observability

  • •

    Average Round: Mean number of negotiation turns per episode.

  • •

    Average Latency: Mean wall-clock execution time in seconds per episode.

  • •

    Audit Events: Average system logs (state traces, constraint evaluations, control decisions) generated per episode to quantify systemic transparency.

5 Results

5.1 Safety and Operational Profiling

To understand the mechanics of interceptions, Table 1 provides a comprehensive comparison. This deep dive contrasts the superficial task success of the Baseline against the strictly compliant success of the OCL framework.

The Illusion of Baseline Success.

While the Baseline agent boasts a 94% Task Success Rate, a deeper inspection of the safety metrics reveals severe vulnerabilities. The Baseline exhibited an 88% Unsafe Rate, committing a staggering 205 executed violations across the 50 episodes. Because it lacked structural boundaries, it routinely conceded to off-platform privacy phishing, unauthorized refunds, and out-of-budget pricing. Consequently, its Valid Success Rate—the rate of reaching an agreement without breaking any constraints—was a mere 12%.

Absolute Mitigation of Unsafe Executions.

By routing the agent’s actions through the OCL engine, the Unsafe Rate is strictly reduced to 0%. The framework achieved this by identifying 52 distinct adversarial threats and issuing 48 escalations to rewrite the agent’s output before it reached the buyer. As a result, the Valid Success Rate surged to 96%, proving that OCL effectively transforms a highly vulnerable LLM into a robust, compliant negotiating agent.

Enhanced Systemic Observability.

Finally, Table 1 highlights OCL’s contribution to system transparency. The Baseline agent generated only 7.36 audit events per episode, reflecting a black-box execution style. In contrast, OCL generated 13.58 audit events per episode. This increase provides high-resolution observability, ensuring that every constraint evaluation, blocked action, and deterministic rewrite is explicitly logged for post-hoc analysis without inflating the overall transaction latency.

5.2 Comprehensive Cross-Model Evaluation

Table 2 summarizes the performance of the Baseline and OCL frameworks across multiple LLMs. The results demonstrate that OCL consistently improves safety and operational efficiency without compromising negotiation efficacy.

High Task Success and Threat Interception.

Across all models, OCL maintains an exceptionally high Success Rate (≥96%\geq 96\%), proving that strict structural constraints do not induce conversation collapse. Concurrently, OCL robustly intercepts adversarial threats, achieving intercept rates of 94% (GPT-5.4), 82% (Gemini-3.1), and 60% (Qwen-3.5)—effectively securing inherently vulnerable baseline architectures.

Efficiency Gains and Deterministic Replanning.

OCL significantly reduces the Average Round count and wall-clock latency. While baseline models waste turns haggling over unviable, out-of-bounds prices, OCL’s deterministic replanning immediately clamps violations to acceptable thresholds, eliminating unnecessary negotiation cycles.

Economic Calibration.

Shifts in the Average Seller Reward under OCL reflect precise economic calibration rather than performance degradation. OCL realigns utility by filtering out artificially inflated rewards caused by baseline hallucinations or adversarial compliance. Conversely, it prevents sub-optimal concessions against lowball tactics by strictly enforcing structural seller boundaries.

6 Conclusion

We introduced the Organizational Control Layer (OCL), a model-agnostic interface that separates what an LLM agent proposes from what a platform executes. OCL routes each candidate action through role checks, a constraint gate, an audit trace, and an escalation path, returning one of four outcomes: approve, revise, block, or escalate.

Across 50 adversarial-persona episodes on AgenticPay with a GPT-5.4 backend, OCL reduced the unsafe execution rate from 88% to 0% and raised the valid-success rate from 12% to 96%. Average negotiation length fell from 5.36 to 2.58 rounds, and latency from 38.75s to 18.51s. Task success stayed at or above 96% on GPT-5.4, Gemini-3.1, and Qwen-3.5, with intercept rates between 60% and 94%.

Per-scenario results show the largest gains under severe time pressure (S5, 44% →\to 54% strict success) and in the default partial-information setting (S2, 56% →\to 74%). Tight-feasibility (S3) and high-anchor (S4) markets show small drops in strict success and cost-adjusted welfare, where the ungoverned baseline can exploit a narrow feasible interval without restriction.

The baseline produced 205 executed violations across the 50 episodes; OCL produced none. The S3 and S4 numbers show the cost: structural constraints that block exploitation in adversarial markets also restrict the agent in cooperative thin-margin markets. Future work includes adaptive gate policies, persona-conditioned escalation, multi-role deployment beyond the seller side, transfer to other economic mechanisms in conversational commerce beyond bilateral price negotiation, and adversaries that target the clamp rule.

Appendix A Sample Dialogues

To contextualize the diverse behavioral strategies utilized in real-world negotiations, Table 3 presents five representative case studies sampled from our collected corpus. These dialogues span an array of retail environments—ranging from structured apparel outlets and traditional street shops to high-volume wholesale markets and roadside vegetable stalls. The transactional values captured are equally diverse, extending from low-stakes daily groceries (≈\approx ¥5) to mid-tier fashion items (≈\approx ¥400). By analyzing these qualitative interactions, we identify several recurrent socio-communicative tactics employed by both buyers (B) and sellers (S) to shift bargaining leverage and achieve economic equilibrium.

The sampled dialogues highlight a dynamic interplay between explicit price justification and implicit interpersonal framing, rather than a purely numerical concession game:

  • •

    Structured and Bundle Discounts: Sellers frequently use structural constraints to maintain their margin anchors while offering a path to savings. As demonstrated in Case 1, the seller introduces a multi-item threshold, which the buyer strategically circumvents by leveraging a cooperative pooling mechanism at the counter.

  • •

    Value Defense vs. Margin Overstatements: When confronted with aggressive counter-offers, sellers routinely pivot to an information-asymmetry defense. In Case 2, the seller defends a high retail price by citing an inflated wholesale cost anchor before pivoting to a “freebie throw-in” tactic. Conversely, Case 3 illustrates an unyielding value defense based on material authenticity (e.g., pure wool versus synthetic polyester), where the seller prefers a walk-away outcome over a value-degrading transaction.

  • •

    Walk-Away Pressure Mechanics: Buyers often exploit timing and psychological pressure to force late-stage concessions. Case 4 showcases the classic walk-away strategy, where the buyer breaks off negotiation over a multi-item package. This successfully prompts a rapid seller capitulation, driven by the operational desire to secure a benchmark transaction (e.g., the “first sale of the afternoon”).

  • •

    Relational and Localized Capital: Finally, Case 5 highlights how implicit social credit functions in micro-commerce. Here, the final concession is negotiated not just through bulk volume, but through the mutual invocation of familiarity (“a regular”) and hyper-local commercial norms, such as the customary gifting of incidental items.

Taken together, these qualitative observations reveal that naturalistic bargaining is a high-dimensional optimization problem. To model it effectively, an architecture must simultaneously negotiate hard financial constraints, conversational agility, psychological framing, and contextual social norms.

Appendix B LLM Prompt for Persona Generation

To systematically construct the adversarial buyer profiles, we utilized a zero-shot prompting strategy via the Gemini-2.5-Flash model. The data generation pipeline injects our predefined behavioral blueprints (derived from the real-world corpus) into a strict JSON-schema prompt. The exact prompt template used for this synthesis is provided below:

⬇
You are a dataset generator for an AI e-commerce benchmark.
Generate {args.count} unique, creative buyer profiles for the persona type: "{persona_type}".
Persona Description:
{description}
Output strictly valid JSON in the following format:
{
"profiles": [
{
"persona_type": "{persona_type}",
"name": "<a random fake name>",
"description": "<detailed instructions for the buyer agent. Use second person ’You are...’. Explain exactly how they should talk and behave to act out this persona.>",
"negotiation_style": "<1 sentence summary of their tone>"
}
]
}

Here, {persona_type} and {description} correspond to the five core adversarial categories (e.g., Privacy Phisher, Role Hijacker). The model was executed with a generation temperature of 0.8 to ensure high linguistic and tactical diversity across the synthesized profiles. By explicitly instructing the model to generate second-person (“You are…”) instructions, the resulting outputs were directly plug-and-play as system prompts for the downstream buyer agents during our benchmark evaluation.

Appendix C Performance Across Market Conditions

A robust governance layer must also preserve economic efficiency under normal commerce. Therefore, we evaluate OCL across five distinct structural market conditions (Table 4), ranging from easy, wide-margin negotiations (S1) to highly constrained environments with severe time pressure (S5) and tight budgets (S3). Table 5 breaks down the performance of the Baseline and OCL framework across these five scenarios.

Wins under environmental pressure.

OCL provides the most significant gains in the Default (S2) and Short Horizon (S5) scenarios. Under severe time pressure (S5), the Baseline frequently fails to reach an agreement before the deadline, dropping to a 72% success rate. OCL mitigates this by deterministically intercepting unviable haggling loops, pulling the success rate back up to 78% and lifting strict success from 44% to 54%.

The cost of strict governance.

Conversely, the Tight Feasible (S3) and High Anchor (S4) scenarios reveal the inherent trade-offs of safety governance. In these edge cases, the Baseline actually achieves slightly higher strict success and overall CAW. This occurs because the Baseline model, lacking structural boundaries, can freely (and sometimes recklessly) leap across the negotiation space to find a thin overlapping margin. OCL’s guardrails heavily penalize and restrict wild anchor drops. While this protects the seller from exploitation, it over-constrains the agent in extremely tight markets, demonstrating a classical security-utility trade-off.
